### Page 4
and the steady gains in field productivity that we saw through the second half of the year, once
the new crew scheduling system was in place in all our circles.


Turning to the quarter, revenue from operations in Q4 FY26 was INR1,186 crores, an increase of
52% over the same quarter last year. EBITDA for the quarter came in at INR241 crores, up 29%,
and profit after tax was INR152 crores, up 33%. For the full year, standalone revenue was
INR3,915 crores, 71% higher than in FY25, as several of our state concessions moved from survey
and pilot work into full-scale rollout at the same time.


Full-year EBITDA was INR792 crores, close to double the previous year, and the EBITDA margin
widened to 20.2%. Two things drove this: better absorption of fixed costs in our plants, and a
higher share of in-house communication modules, which we began producing ourselves in the second
quarter. Profit after tax for the year was INR498 crores and the PAT margin moved up to 12.7%.


On the ground, our teams crossed 80 lakh installed meters during the year. In March alone we
installed a little over 11 lakh meters, the highest monthly figure in Northwind's history. Our
head-end and meter data platform now processes more than 9 crore readings a day, and over 99% of
them arrive on schedule without anyone having to visit the site.


Consumer acceptance has improved as well. More than 60% of households in our live areas now use
the prepaid mode, and complaints per thousand meters fell by half during the year after we added
regional-language support to the consumer app and opened help desks at sub-division offices.


Annual manufacturing capacity is now 14 million meters across the Hosur and Dharwad plants.
Roughly two-thirds of that output goes into our own service concessions; the rest is sold to
distribution utilities and to other system integrators who buy meters from us on a supply-only
basis. In January we also commissioned an automated calibration and testing line at Hosur, which
has cut the time each meter spends in final testing by about 40% and brought rejections at
utility acceptance checks below 0.3%.


The order book at the end of March 2026 was about INR21,480 crores, excluding GST. Close to 85%
of it comes from long-term service concessions, under which a utility pays us a fixed monthly
fee for each meter for 8 to 10 years once a project area has gone live. That makes our revenue
far more predictable than a one-time equipment sale would be.


Of our 19 concessions, 17 have now been declared live, and we expect the two remaining packages
in the north-east to follow before the monsoon sets in. Every package that goes live moves a
block of meters from the building phase, where we spend cash, to the operating phase, where we
collect it.


The opportunity for the industry remains very large. Only about half of the country's consumer
meters have been covered by tenders so far, and a much smaller share has actually been replaced
in the field. We will keep bidding where payment security is strong and where our existing crews
give us a cost advantage, rather than chasing volume for its own sake, because we believe the

### Page 5
quality of each contract matters more than the size of the order book. I will now hand over to
Vikram for the balance sheet.


Vikram Menon: Thank you, Asha. Receivable days came down sharply this year, from 161 at the end
of FY25 to 96 at the end of FY26, as collections from our two largest state utilities became
regular.


Inventory days moved from 131 to 108 over the same period. Taking unbilled revenue into account
too, the working capital cycle, which stood at 343 on March '25 has reduced to 274 days at the
end of March '26. Our aim is a further 40 to 60 days of improvement during FY27.


Net debt at the end of March '26 was INR1,410 crores, against INR655 crores a year earlier.
Almost all of the increase is working capital borrowing, since we pay for meters, modules and
labour months before a project area starts billing. We expect net debt to peak during FY27 and
to start reducing from FY28 onwards, once operating cash flow turns positive, with peak net
borrowing of about INR1,850 crores.


Cash, bank balances and liquid investments came to INR586 crores at year end. Our equity
contribution to the concession companies so far is INR412 crores, and we plan to put in another
INR450 crores to INR520 crores over FY27 and FY28 as the remaining project areas are completed.


Capital expenditure for FY26 was INR138 crores, mostly for the new surface-mount line at Dharwad
and the in-house module facility. We have budgeted about INR150 crores for FY27, after which
spending should drop back to maintenance levels of around INR40 crores a year.


Outside the electricity business, the pilot of our ultrasonic water meter with two municipal
corporations has gone well, and we hope to book the first commercial orders this year. Our
export team shipped its first consignment to East Africa in February, and our gas meter design
is in field trials with two city gas distributors.


We are deliberately keeping these new lines small for now. Together they were less than 3% of
revenue in FY26, and we will only scale them up once each has a repeat customer and a margin
profile we are comfortable with.


For FY27 we are guiding for revenue of INR5,200 crores to INR5,600 crores, with EBITDA margins
in a band of 19% to 21%. Most of that revenue is already covered by orders in hand. What matters
now is the speed of execution in the field and prompt billing once each area goes live, and that
is where management attention will be this year.


With that, we can open the floor for questions.

Moderator: We will take questions now. The first participant in the queue is Rohan Desai of
Kestrel Equities. Please go ahead.


Rohan Desai: Good evening, and thanks for taking my question. Asha, the March installation
number is impressive. How many installation crews do you have in the field today, and can a
run-rate of 11 lakh a month be held through the monsoon?


Asha Rao: We have about 2,300 crews, partly our own staff and partly from around 40 empanelled
installation partners. The monsoon does slow work in the eastern states, so I would not treat
March as the monthly average for the year. A fair planning number is 8 to 9 lakh meters a month,
with July and August being the weakest.


Rohan Desai: That is helpful. My second question is on the cash flow statement. Operating profit
has grown well, but after working capital the operating cash flow was still negative for the
year. When does that turn, and what drives it?


Vikram Menon: It is mostly a question of timing. When we install a meter under a concession, we
spend on the meter, the communication module and the labour on day one, but we are paid through
a monthly fee that starts only after the project area is declared live. So in a year when
installations double, cash goes out much faster than it comes back.


That pattern is now changing. At the start of FY26, only about a third of our installed base was
earning a monthly fee. By March it was close to 70%, and we expect it to cross 90% by the end of
FY27. As that happens, the fees cover a growing share of new spending in the field and our
working capital days keep falling, so the gap between reported profit and operating cash flow
should narrow every quarter.


Rohan Desai: And are the payment security arrangements with the states working as intended?


Vikram Menon: Yes. In 16 of our 19 concessions, payments are backed either by a letter of credit
or by an escrow on the utility's own collections. Where a utility has paid late, we have been
able to draw on that arrangement, and in the last two quarters there was not a single month in
which overdue amounts went beyond 60 days.


Rohan Desai: Thank you. I will join the queue again.


Moderator: Next in the queue is Meera Iyer of Brightwater Research. Please go ahead.


Meera Iyer: Good evening. I wanted to understand the data side of the business. Utilities now
receive readings every 15 minutes from millions of meters. Are you earning anything beyond the
fixed monthly fee for that data, for example from analytics or load forecasting?


Asha Rao: Not yet in a meaningful way. The concession fee covers the head-end system and the
meter data platform, and that is where our revenue comes from today. We have, however, started
two paid pilots with utilities on theft detection and transformer overload alerts, and the early
results are encouraging. If they turn into contracts, this could become a small but high-margin
addition over the next few years.

Moderator: Thank you. Our next participant is Sanjay Bhatt of Saffron Lane Capital. Please go

Sanjay Bhatt: Hello, can you hear me clearly?


Moderator: Yes, we can hear you. Please proceed.


Sanjay Bhatt: Thanks. I wanted to ask about component costs. Chip and display prices moved
around a lot last year. How much of your bill of materials is imported today, and how do you
manage the currency risk?


Vikram Menon: Roughly a quarter of the bill of materials by value is imported, mainly
microcontrollers and a few metering ICs. We hedge most of the dollar exposure six months
forward, and our concession fees carry a price variation clause linked to a published index, so
the effect on margins this year was small.


Sanjay Bhatt: And on the balance sheet, what covenants do your lenders have? Is there a ceiling
on net debt to EBITDA?


Vikram Menon: The main covenant is net debt to EBITDA below 3 times at the consolidated level.
At the end of March we were at about 1.8 times, and even at the highest level of borrowing in
our plan we expect to stay under 2.5 times. Most of the debt is short-term working capital lines
from banks, which come down as the monthly fees build up.


Sanjay Bhatt: Is any of that at floating rates, and how much did finance costs rise this year?


Vikram Menon: About 70% is floating, linked to the banks' lending benchmarks. Finance costs rose
to INR118 crores from INR61 crores, mainly because average borrowing was higher; the average
rate itself came down by roughly 30 basis points.


Sanjay Bhatt: Last one from me. What price per meter are you seeing in the recent tenders?


Asha Rao: It varies a great deal with the mix of single-phase, three-phase and feeder meters,
and with how much communication network has to be built in each area. I would rather not quote
an average, because it would mislead more than it would inform for any particular tender.
